Memory.Wiki's structural wedge is **cross-AI memory** — a layer that giants (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) cannot build because of their own competitive incentives.

## The core argument

> "Any single AI company is structurally incentivized *not* to build this themselves."

- OpenAI won't ship memory that's fetchable by Anthropic
- Anthropic won't ship memory that serves ChatGPT
- A vendor building cross-AI memory would mean shipping a feature that helps competitors — a competitive own-goal

So the cross-AI layer can only be built by a neutral independent. That's the gap Memory.Wiki occupies.

## Why this matters

Today's AI users live across 5+ tools (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Cursor, MCP hosts). Each has isolated memory islands. Every tool switch = re-explaining context.

Memory.Wiki's answer: **one URL any AI can fetch**. Knowledge lives outside any single vendor's walls, as markdown over HTTPS — the simplest universal interface.

## Internal vs external framing

- **Internal thesis**: "Cross-AI is structurally impossible for giants. The graph is the product."
- **External thesis** (user-facing): "Stop re-explaining your context to every AI."

The wedge is positioning, not headcount — which is why a solo founder can build it in months while giants structurally cannot.

Memory.Wiki’s wedge is **cross-AI context portability**.

Single-AI memory systems — ChatGPT Memory, Claude Projects, Gemini saved context, etc. — are locked inside one vendor. ChatGPT’s memory helps ChatGPT, but not Claude or Cursor. Claude’s memory helps Claude, but not ChatGPT.

Memory.Wiki sits outside those silos:

> **One URL every AI can read.**

Its structural advantage is that OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and similar vendors are not incentivized to build a neutral memory layer that also helps their competitors. OpenAI will not build memory optimized for Claude; Anthropic will not build memory optimized for ChatGPT. That makes **cross-AI memory structurally hard for giants to ship**, but natural for an independent layer.

Memory.Wiki turns user-authored knowledge into markdown URLs — doc, bundle, or user/hub — that any AI can fetch. The AI receives organized context, not just raw notes.

So the wedge is:

> **Your context lives outside any one AI, as a URL, portable across ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Gemini, and future tools.**

Internally: “The graph is the product.”  
Externally: “Stop re-explaining your context to every AI.”

Memory.Wiki's structural wedge is its **cross-AI delivery layer**. 

While giant AI companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are building their own memory systems (e.g., ChatGPT Memory, Claude Projects), these are closed systems locked to their specific platforms. 

Memory.Wiki's structural advantage is that these tech giants are structurally incentivized *not* to build a cross-AI memory layer. For example, if OpenAI created a memory system that seamlessly delivered context to Claude, it would be helping a direct competitor—a "competitive own-goal." Because AI giants cannot build a memory layer that serves their competitors without undermining their own ecosystems, this cross-AI layer must come from an independent, neutral third party. 

By using a universal markdown URL that any AI (ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Gemini) can fetch and read, Memory.Wiki fills this gap. This cross-AI portability allows users to stop re-explaining their context to every new tool, creating a structural moat that single-AI vendors cannot replicate.

Based on the hub content, Hyunsang Cho is building memory.wiki for several interconnected reasons:

**The core problem he saw:** Every day people pour valuable thinking into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Cursor — then close the tab and lose it. The next day they re-explain who they are, what they're working on, what they already decided. He calls this "the most expensive forgetting machine."

**The key insight (from his Humain experience):** While leading product at Saudi Arabia's national AI program, he saw that the real question isn't "is our model good enough?" but "what layer can we own that big labs don't?" He identified that cross-AI memory is structurally impossible for OpenAI or Anthropic to build — they can't ship a memory layer serving their competitors. So it has to come from outside.

**His thesis:** The answer is a URL. Knowledge as a markdown URL any AI can fetch. Layer 3 (memory protocol) sits empty between models and applications — neither model companies nor app companies can fill it without conflicts. A neutral startup must define this standard, similar to how RSS, OAuth, and Open Graph emerged.

**Personal motivation:** He wanted his AI tools to share his knowledge across ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor. Every existing solution was a closed memory.

**The vision:** A sustainable craftsman SaaS — "Stop re-explaining your context to every AI. Put your knowledge in one URL they can all read." Target: $2-5M ARR in 5 years, 1k-10k users who genuinely love the product.

Hyunsang Cho is building Memory.Wiki because he believes the real problem is not “AI memory,” but **knowledge delivery**.

People pour useful context, decisions, code, and strategy into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Cursor, then lose functional access to it. The next day they must re-explain who they are, what they’re working on, and what they already decided.

Existing memory systems are closed: ChatGPT Memory helps ChatGPT, Claude Projects help Claude, Notion stays inside Notion, local files stay local. Hyunsang’s thesis is that knowledge should live as a **URL any AI can read**.

- one doc: `memory.wiki/<id>`

His deeper bet is that **cross-AI memory is structurally hard for giants to build**, because OpenAI will not build memory for Claude, and Anthropic will not build memory for ChatGPT.

mdfy’s retrieval is built around its memory graph, not just “RAG UI.”

Core pieces:

- **Markdown is source of truth** in `documents.markdown`.
- On document save, mdfy creates embeddings for:
  - the whole document
  - heading-aware document chunks
  - bundles
- Embeddings live in Postgres/pgvector:
  - `documents.embedding`
  - `bundles.embedding`
  - `document_chunks.embedding`
- Re-embedding is skipped when content has not changed via `embedding_source_hash`.

Retrieval happens mainly through MCP tools such as `mdfy_search` / memory search:

- The AI queries your library by meaning, not just keywords.
- Search uses vector similarity over docs/chunks/bundles.
- Some docs describe this as vector + BM25 hybrid recall with paragraph-level chunks.

For AI consumption, mdfy often avoids raw retrieval entirely: Doc, Bundle, and Hub URLs return pre-organized markdown. Bundle and Hub payloads include AI-generated summaries, concepts, relations, and links, so the receiving AI gets a navigable context map instead of random chunks.

So: embeddings power semantic recall, while URLs deliver the organized graph as context.

Based on the provided content, mdfy frames its RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline as "mdfy Memory." It utilizes a chunked and hybrid retrieval approach (combining vector similarity and BM25) to power semantic search. 

Here is how the retrieval process works:

*   **Embedding & Chunking:** When a document is saved, the `/api/embed/<id>` pipeline automatically embeds the title and full markdown body for global search. It also breaks the document down, chunking each section (or paragraph) individually for finer recall.
*   **Storage:** The vectors are stored using `pgvector` across specific database tables (`documents.embedding`, `bundles.embedding`, and `document_chunks.embedding`). To optimize costs, an `embedding_source_hash` ensures unchanged content isn't re-embedded.
*   **Retrieval:** AI models access this data via the `/recall` API or the `mdfy_search` tool within mdfy's MCP server. This allows the AI to perform true semantic recall (e.g., "which docs cover X?") based on vector similarity and meaning, rather than relying solely on exact keyword matches.

Based on the document "How mdfy keeps your docs, bundles, and hub fresh," mdfy uses three layers with different freshness strategies:

**1. Document body — always fresh (automatic)**
- New markdown is in Postgres immediately on save
- AI URLs see updates within ~60 seconds via `/raw/{id}` and `/d/{id}` (read straight from DB)
- Edge cache uses `stale-while-revalidate=300` but revalidates in background
- No action needed

**2. Bundle graph — manual re-analyze**
- AI-generated themes/insights are computed once and stamped with `graph_generated_at`
- Compared against `embedding_updated_at` of member docs
- If a member doc changes, bundle becomes stale and shows "Re-analyze with AI" button
- Not auto-rebuilt because LLM calls cost tokens and could disrupt editing

**3. Hub concept index — automatic + manual top-up**
- Every doc save fires: enqueue ontology job → fast-path LLM extraction (seconds) → cron backstop if instance dies
- Two guardrails: 30-minute per-doc cooldown and 200-character minimum delta (control costs)
- A "Re-analyze (N)" banner appears when `docs_touched_at > concepts_built_at`
- Manual click only re-extracts changed docs (capped at 50/click), bypasses cooldown, runs asynchronously
- Doc-level re-analyze also available via right-click

The design philosophy: aggressive freshness for body markdown (no click needed), but explicit user control for costly AI-derived metadata.

mdfy uses different freshness rules for each layer:

| Layer | Freshness model |
|---|---|
| **Document body** | Always fresh. Saves write markdown to Postgres immediately, and AI-facing URLs update within ~60 seconds. No user action needed. |
| **Bundle graph** | Generated once by AI, then reused. If a member doc changes after `graph_generated_at`, the bundle becomes stale and shows `analysis_stale: true` plus a **“Re-analyze with AI”** option. |
| **Hub concept index** | Mostly automatic. Each doc save enqueues an ontology refresh job; concepts usually update within seconds, with cron retry if serverless execution fails. |

For hubs, mdfy has two cost-control guardrails:

- **30-minute cooldown per doc** so active editing doesn’t burn LLM calls.
- **200-character minimum delta** so typo fixes don’t trigger extraction.

If the hub detects changed docs after the last concept build, it shows a **“Concepts out of date · Re-analyze (N)”** banner. Clicking it only re-extracts changed docs, caps at 50 docs per click, and bypasses the cooldown.

So: markdown stays fresh automatically; AI-derived metadata is fast by default, but explicitly refreshable.

Based on the provided content, mdfy maintains freshness across its three layers using a mix of automatic updates and manual controls to balance accuracy and AI costs:

*   **Documents (Body):** Always fresh. When you save a document, the new markdown is updated in the database and propagates to AI URLs within approximately 60 seconds. No manual action is required.
*   **Bundles (AI Graph):** AI-generated themes and insights remain up-to-date until a member document's content changes. When this happens, the bundle is marked as "stale," and a "Re-analyze with AI" button appears. Users must manually click this to rebuild the graph, which prevents unwanted token usage and disruptions during active editing.
*   **Hubs (Concept Index):** Concepts are automatically extracted within seconds of a save, but there is a 30-minute cooldown per document to control costs. If heavy editing causes the hub's concept map to fall out of sync, a yellow "Re-analyze (N)" banner appears. Clicking it bypasses the cooldown and only re-extracts the specific documents that changed (capped at 50 per click). 

You can also right-click a single document to force a concept refresh at any time.
